in_text_mentions: Our patient had pronounced difficulty in walking and speaking. Extraoral examination revealed exophthalmia and xerophthalmia. Telangiectasia of the face and compressed nose were found (Figure 1). Dermatological findings included macular lesions on the forearm and the front part of the chest, as well as hyperkeratotic depigmented areas on the palms and foot (Figures 2(a), 2(b), and 2(c)).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real patient AP elbow radiograph from a young adult male with Rothmund-Thomson syndrome (explicit caption history plus disease-focused article title on low-energy long bone fractures in RTS). The panel visibly shows a mildly displaced low-energy olecranon fracture (the article's central manifestation) and a congenital radial head–proximal ulna fusion, i.e., a radial ray anomaly tagged under the RTS radial ray defect vocabulary. White and grey arrow annotations are present. B: Lateral elbow radiograph of the same RTS patient; better depicts the mildly displaced olecranon fracture with osteolysis and cortication at the fracture margins (raised concern for a lytic lesion, but biopsy was negative for neoplasm and infection, so not tagged as osteosarcoma) and repeats the congenital radial head–ulna fusion, a radial ray anomaly. Oval and grey-arrow annotations are present.
panels.attribution_text: Beckmann. Multiple Low Energy Long Bone Fractures in the Setting of Rothmund-Thomson Syndrome.. Case reports in medicine 2015. doi:10.1155/2015/495164. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Young adult male with history of Rothmund-Thomson syndrome diagnosed at 2 years of age. Findings: (a) mildly displaced fracture through the olecranon (white arrow). There is congenital fusion of radial head and proximal ulna (grey arrow). (b) The mildly displaced olecranon is better appreciated on the lateral radiograph. There is osteolysis and cortication along the fracture margins (oval), which raised the concern for underlying lytic bone lesion. Congenital fusion of the radial head and ulna is again noted (grey arrow). Technique: (a) AP radiograph kVp = 65, mAs = 4, and (b) Lateral radiograph kVp = 65, mAs = 4.
in_text_mentions: ter for treatment of a left olecranon fracture sustained during a fall playing soccer 3.5 weeks earlier. Presenting radiographs showed a mildly displaced subacute fracture through the left olecranon (Figure 4). There was early cortication along the fracture margins and more osteolysis than expected along the fracture line given the reported age of the fracture. Therefore, a bone biopsy of the fracture was performed, which was negative for neoplasm and infection. Tension band wiring of the olecranon fracture was subsequently performed (Figure 5). source_variant.figure_caption: Young adult male with history of Rothmund-Thomson syndrome diagnosed at 2 years of age. Findings: (a) mildly displaced fracture through the olecranon (white arrow). There is congenital fusion of radial head and proximal ulna (grey arrow). (b) The mildly displaced olecranon is better appreciated on the lateral radiograph. There is osteolysis and cortication along the fracture margins (oval), which raised the concern for underlying lytic bone lesion. Congenital fusion of the radial head and ulna is again noted (grey arrow). Technique: (a) AP radiograph kVp = 65, mAs = 4, and (b) Lateral radiograph kVp = 65, mAs = 4.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of the left hand in a 34-year-old adult with confirmed Rothmund-Thomson syndrome. Caption notes relatively small hands with small though normally shaped nails and normal thumbs, consistent with the patient's documented short stature. Thumb hypoplasia (a classic RTS finding) is explicitly absent, making this a variant presentation. Skin is visibly light-toned. B: Clinical photograph of the right hand in a 34-year-old adult with confirmed Rothmund-Thomson syndrome. Caption notes relatively small hands with small though normally shaped nails and normal thumbs, consistent with the patient's documented short stature. Thumb hypoplasia (a classic RTS finding) is explicitly absent, making this a variant presentation. Skin is visibly light-toned.

in_text_mentions: ion showed a slender man with a short stature (height 167 cm, (−2.1 SDS), with a saddle nose, absence of eyelashes and eyebrows and facial poikiloderma, (Fig. 1). He had sparse hair on the scalp, with two spots of alopecia areata and multiple small hyperpigmented macules on the trunk and arms. He had small but normal hands (Fig. 2); at the right foot, a partial 2–3 syndactyly of the right foot was observed.Fig. 1Facial features at age 34. Note: absent eye brows and eye lashes, small nose Fig. 2Hands at age 34. Note: relatively small hands, with small though normally shaped nails, normal thumbs

plate_findings.evidence: Caption: "Poikiloderma in a patient with RTS. Depigmentation, hyperpigmentation, punctate atrophy, telangiectasia, and loss of eyebrows are seen bilaterally on the face."; in-text: bilateral depigmentation, hyperpigmentation, punctate atrophy, and telangiectasia over the patient's face and ears (Fig. 1)

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left oblique clinical photograph of a young child's face from a case report of Rothmund-Thomson syndrome with novel compound heterozygous RECQL4 mutations; the caption explicitly attributes the bilateral facial depigmentation, hyperpigmentation, punctate atrophy, telangiectasia and eyebrow loss to RTS, matching the textbook facial poikiloderma finding. Real patient image, adequately lit, disease attribution unambiguous. B: Right oblique clinical photograph of the same child's face from the RTS case report, showing the bilateral facial poikiloderma (depigmentation, hyperpigmentation, punctate atrophy, telangiectasia) and eyebrow loss described in the caption and in-text; clear untreated disease manifestation of the configured target disease.
